question: An elderly patient has exertional syncope and a harsh systolic murmur radiating to the neck. Which valvular lesion best explains his presentation?
cited_learning_objective: Outline the pathogenesis, etiologies, and clinical and morphologic findings of aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation, mitral valve prolapse, mitral regurgitation, and mitral stenosis

options.text: Calcific degeneration of aortic valve cusps
options.rationale: Calcific degeneration of aortic valve cusps causes progressive narrowing of the orifice producing exertional angina, syncope, and a crescendo–decrescendo systolic ejection murmur radiating to the carotids, as described in the lecture.

options.text: Myxomatous degeneration of mitral valve leaflets
options.rationale: Myxomatous degeneration causes mitral valve prolapse and mid-systolic click with possible regurgitation; it would not produce a systolic ejection murmur radiating to the neck. It would be correct if the murmur were a late systolic murmur with a click.

options.text: Rheumatic fusion of mitral valve commissures
options.rationale: Rheumatic commissural fusion produces mitral stenosis with diastolic murmur and opening snap, not a systolic ejection murmur radiating to the carotids. It would be correct if the patient had pulmonary congestion and diastolic findings.

options.text: Aortic root dilation causing leaflet separation
options.rationale: Aortic root dilation leads to aortic regurgitation with early diastolic decrescendo murmur and wide pulse pressure, not a systolic ejection murmur with carotid radiation. It would be correct if diastolic findings and increased pulse pressure were present.

options.text: Infective destruction of aortic valve cusps
options.rationale: Acute infective destruction can cause severe regurgitation and acute heart failure rather than a chronic systolic ejection murmur with concentric LV hypertrophy; it would be correct if there were fever, large vegetations, and rapid deterioration.

question: A 30-year-old woman has a mid-systolic click followed by a late systolic murmur. Which underlying valve pathology most likely produces these auscultatory findings?
cited_learning_objective: Outline the pathogenesis, etiologies, and clinical and morphologic findings of aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation, mitral valve prolapse, mitral regurgitation, and mitral stenosis

options.text: Myxomatous degeneration with redundant mitral leaflets
options.rationale: Myxomatous degeneration causes leaflet thickening and interchordal ballooning producing a mid-systolic click and late systolic murmur from mitral regurgitation, as noted in the lecture.

options.text: Calcific nodules on aortic valve cusps
options.rationale: Calcific nodules on aortic cusps cause a systolic ejection murmur of aortic stenosis, not a mid-systolic click with late systolic murmur. It would be correct if carotid radiation and LV hypertrophy were present.

options.text: Commissural fusion of mitral valve leaflets
options.rationale: Commissural fusion from rheumatic disease causes mitral stenosis with diastolic murmur and opening snap, not a mid-systolic click. It would be correct if diastolic findings and left atrial enlargement were present.

options.text: Papillary muscle rupture after myocardial infarction
options.rationale: Papillary muscle rupture causes acute severe mitral regurgitation with holosystolic murmur and pulmonary edema, not a mid-systolic click with late systolic murmur. It would be correct if acute pulmonary edema and new holosystolic murmur occurred.

options.text: Nonbacterial sterile thrombotic vegetations on valves
options.rationale: NBTE produces small bland vegetations and embolic risk but does not characteristically cause a mid-systolic click or late systolic murmur; it would be correct if the patient had a hypercoagulable state and systemic emboli without valve prolapse signs.

question: Which physical finding is most characteristic of chronic aortic regurgitation?
cited_learning_objective: Outline the pathogenesis, etiologies, and clinical and morphologic findings of aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation, mitral valve prolapse, mitral regurgitation, and mitral stenosis

options.text: Wide pulse pressure with early diastolic murmur
options.rationale: Chronic aortic regurgitation causes volume overload producing increased stroke volume and widened pulse pressure and an early blowing decrescendo diastolic murmur, as described in the lecture.

options.text: Narrow pulse pressure with systolic ejection murmur
options.rationale: Narrow pulse pressure with systolic ejection murmur is more consistent with severe aortic stenosis and low output states; it would be correct if the patient had concentric LV hypertrophy and reduced stroke volume.

options.text: Mid-systolic click with late systolic murmur
options.rationale: A mid-systolic click with late systolic murmur indicates mitral valve prolapse from myxomatous degeneration, not aortic regurgitation. It would be correct if auscultation revealed a click and late murmur.

options.text: Diastolic rumble with opening snap after S2
options.rationale: A diastolic rumble with opening snap is characteristic of mitral stenosis due to chronic rheumatic disease, not aortic regurgitation. It would be correct if left atrial enlargement and pulmonary hypertension were present.

options.text: Holosystolic blowing murmur at apex radiating
options.rationale: A holosystolic blowing murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla indicates mitral regurgitation, not aortic regurgitation. It would be correct if regurgitant flow into the left atrium were documented.

question: Which histologic feature is diagnostic of acute rheumatic myocarditis?
cited_learning_objective: List the diagnostic criteria of acute rheumatic fever; describe the pathogenesis and gross/histologic findings of acute and chronic rheumatic heart disease

options.text: Aschoff bodies with Anitschkow caterpillar cells
options.rationale: Aschoff bodies containing activated macrophages and Anitschkow 'caterpillar' cells are characteristic histologic findings of acute rheumatic myocarditis, as stated in the lecture.

options.text: Granulomas with caseous necrosis in myocardium
options.rationale: Granulomas with caseous necrosis suggest tuberculosis or sarcoidosis, not acute rheumatic myocarditis; it would be correct if acid-fast bacilli or granulomatous inflammation were present.

options.text: Bacterial colonies with abundant neutrophilic infiltrate
options.rationale: Bacterial colonies with neutrophils indicate infective endocarditis or bacterial myocarditis, not rheumatic myocarditis; it would be correct if cultures were positive and vegetations were seen.

options.text: Fibrinoid necrosis with small verrucous vegetations
options.rationale: Fibrinoid necrosis with small verrucous vegetations describes rheumatic endocarditis but is not the specific histologic hallmark of myocarditis; it would be correct if the question asked about valvular lesions in ARF.

options.text: Myxomatous proteoglycan accumulation in leaflets
options.rationale: Myxomatous proteoglycan accumulation characterizes mitral valve prolapse, not acute rheumatic myocarditis; it would be correct if the stem described floppy mitral leaflets and mid-systolic click.

question: Which set of Jones criteria findings would meet the diagnosis of acute rheumatic fever after documented streptococcal infection?
cited_learning_objective: List the diagnostic criteria of acute rheumatic fever; describe the pathogenesis and gross/histologic findings of acute and chronic rheumatic heart disease

options.text: Carditis and migratory polyarthritis as major criteria
options.rationale: Jones criteria require two major or one major plus two minor findings after evidence of prior group A strep; carditis and migratory polyarthritis are both major criteria fulfilling the diagnosis, per the lecture.

options.text: Fever and prolonged PR interval as major criteria
options.rationale: Fever and prolonged PR interval are minor criteria, not major; this option would be correct only if they were accompanied by one major criterion or additional minor criteria to meet the diagnostic threshold.

options.text: Erythema marginatum and chorea as minor criteria
options.rationale: Erythema marginatum and chorea are major criteria, not minor; this option would be correct if the question misclassified major versus minor criteria, which it does not.

options.text: Subcutaneous nodules and arthralgia as minor criteria
options.rationale: Subcutaneous nodules are a major criterion while arthralgia is a minor criterion; this pairing would be correct only if nodules were reclassified as minor, which contradicts the Jones criteria.

options.text: Roth spots and Janeway lesions as major criteria
options.rationale: Roth spots and Janeway lesions are associated with infective endocarditis and are not part of the Jones criteria for rheumatic fever; this would be correct only in the context of bacterial endocarditis.

question: A patient with mitral stenosis is at highest risk for which complication due to left atrial enlargement?
cited_learning_objective: Outline the pathogenesis, etiologies, and clinical and morphologic findings of aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation, mitral valve prolapse, mitral regurgitation, and mitral stenosis

options.text: Atrial fibrillation with thromboembolic stroke risk
options.rationale: Mitral stenosis causes left atrial dilation leading to atrial fibrillation and stasis with increased risk of thrombus formation and systemic embolization, as emphasized in the lecture.

options.text: Right ventricular infarction from coronary occlusion
options.rationale: Right ventricular infarction results from coronary artery occlusion, unrelated to left atrial enlargement from mitral stenosis; it would be correct if there were acute coronary ischemia.

options.text: Pulmonary embolism from deep venous thrombosis
options.rationale: Pulmonary embolism arises from venous thromboembolism, not left atrial thrombi; it would be correct if thrombi originated in the venous system rather than the left atrium.

options.text: Aortic dissection due to hypertension and dilation
options.rationale: Aortic dissection is related to aortic pathology and hypertension, not a direct consequence of mitral stenosis and left atrial enlargement; it would be correct if the patient had aortic root disease.

options.text: Tricuspid regurgitation from annular calcification
options.rationale: Tricuspid regurgitation from annular calcification is uncommon and not the primary risk of left atrial enlargement; it would be correct if there were right-sided valvular disease causing regurgitation.

question: Which organism is most commonly associated with subacute infective endocarditis on previously damaged valves?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the pathogenesis, etiologies, predisposing factors, diagnostic criteria and gross/histologic findings of infective endocarditis

options.text: Streptococcus viridans group oral streptococci
options.rationale: Streptococcus viridans is classically associated with subacute endocarditis on previously damaged valves following transient bacteremia, as noted in the lecture.

options.text: Staphylococcus aureus causing acute destructive endocarditis
options.rationale: Staphylococcus aureus typically causes acute, rapidly progressive endocarditis on normal valves; it would be correct if the stem described a fulminant course with high virulence.

options.text: Staphylococcus epidermidis on native undamaged valves
options.rationale: Staphylococcus epidermidis is associated with prosthetic valve endocarditis rather than native damaged valves; it would be correct if the patient had a prosthetic valve.

options.text: HACEK organisms causing culture negative endocarditis
options.rationale: HACEK organisms can cause endocarditis and are fastidious, but they are less common than S. viridans for subacute disease on damaged valves; it would be correct if cultures were negative and HACEK risk factors present.

options.text: Candida species in immunocompetent community patients
options.rationale: Candida causes fungal endocarditis mainly in immunocompromised or intravenous drug users, not commonly in immunocompetent patients with subacute native valve disease; it would be correct if immunosuppression or fungemia were present.

question: Which major Duke criterion is required for a definitive diagnosis of infective endocarditis when combined with one minor criterion?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the pathogenesis, etiologies, predisposing factors, diagnostic criteria and gross/histologic findings of infective endocarditis

options.text: Positive blood cultures meeting major criterion
options.rationale: A major Duke criterion is persistently positive blood cultures for typical organisms; one major plus three minor or two major plus one minor are diagnostic, per the lecture.

options.text: New conduction block on electrocardiogram tracing
options.rationale: A new conduction block is not a Duke major criterion; it may suggest perivalvular extension but would only support diagnosis indirectly. It would be correct if echocardiographic evidence of abscess were present.

options.text: Single positive blood culture for skin contaminant
options.rationale: A single culture for a likely contaminant does not meet the major criterion; it would be correct only if multiple cultures grew the same organism consistent with endocarditis.

options.text: Fever above 38 degrees Celsius as major criterion
options.rationale: Fever is a minor Duke criterion, not a major one; it would be correct if combined with other major criteria per the diagnostic schema.

options.text: Janeway lesions as a major diagnostic criterion
options.rationale: Janeway lesions are a minor clinical sign in the Duke criteria, not a major criterion; they would support diagnosis as a minor feature alongside major criteria.

question: Which gross valve appearance is most typical for chronic rheumatic mitral stenosis?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the pathogenesis, etiologies, predisposing factors, diagnostic criteria and gross/histologic findings of infective endocarditis

options.text: Commissural fusion producing fish mouth orifice
options.rationale: Chronic rheumatic heart disease causes commissural fusion and thickening of mitral leaflets producing a 'fish mouth' stenotic orifice, as described in the lecture.

options.text: Nodular calcific deposits sparing cusp free edges
options.rationale: Nodular calcific deposits with spared free edges describe degenerative aortic stenosis in elderly patients, not rheumatic mitral stenosis; it would be correct if the valve were aortic and elderly changes present.

options.text: Interchordal ballooning of posterior leaflet
options.rationale: Interchordal ballooning is characteristic of mitral valve prolapse from myxomatous degeneration, not chronic rheumatic stenosis; it would be correct if a mid-systolic click were present.

options.text: Large friable vegetations with cusp destruction
options.rationale: Large friable vegetations with cusp destruction indicate acute infective endocarditis, not chronic rheumatic stenosis; it would be correct if there were fever and positive blood cultures.

options.text: Small sterile verrucous vegetations along closure line
options.rationale: Small verrucous vegetations are seen in acute rheumatic fever and Libman-Sacks endocarditis, but chronic rheumatic stenosis is defined by fibrosis and commissural fusion; this would be correct if the question asked about acute rheumatic valvulitis.

question: Which pathophysiologic change results from chronic aortic stenosis and explains exertional angina?
cited_learning_objective: Understand the basic principles of stenotic and regurgitant valvular lesions

options.text: Concentric left ventricular hypertrophy increasing oxygen demand
options.rationale: Aortic stenosis causes pressure overload leading to concentric LV hypertrophy which increases myocardial oxygen demand and can produce exertional angina, as taught in the lecture.

options.text: Left ventricular dilation reducing systolic ejection fraction
options.rationale: Left ventricular dilation is more typical of volume overload states like chronic regurgitation; it would be correct if the lesion were chronic aortic regurgitation rather than stenosis.

options.text: Left atrial enlargement causing pulmonary congestion
options.rationale: Left atrial enlargement and pulmonary congestion are consequences of mitral stenosis or severe mitral regurgitation, not the primary mechanism for angina in aortic stenosis; it would be correct if mitral valve disease were present.

options.text: Aortic root dilation causing coronary ostial obstruction
options.rationale: Aortic root dilation can affect coronary ostia and cause ischemia but is not the typical mechanism in calcific aortic stenosis; it would be correct if imaging showed root dilation compressing coronary origins.

options.text: Microangiopathic hemolysis producing anemia and ischemia
options.rationale: Microangiopathic hemolysis with schistocytes can occur in severe aortic stenosis but anemia is not the main cause of exertional angina; it would be correct if significant hemolytic anemia were documented causing decreased oxygen delivery.

question: A patient with advanced mitral regurgitation develops volume overload. Which cardiac remodeling pattern is expected?
cited_learning_objective: Understand the basic principles of stenotic and regurgitant valvular lesions

options.text: Left ventricular dilation with eccentric hypertrophy pattern
options.rationale: Chronic mitral regurgitation causes volume overload leading to LV dilation and eccentric hypertrophy to accommodate increased end-diastolic volume, as described in the lecture.

options.text: Concentric hypertrophy with reduced chamber size
options.rationale: Concentric hypertrophy with reduced chamber size results from pressure overload such as aortic stenosis, not volume overload from mitral regurgitation; it would be correct if the lesion were pressure overload.

options.text: Left atrial contraction causing systolic click
options.rationale: Left atrial contraction does not cause a systolic click; a mid-systolic click arises from mitral valve prolapse due to leaflet redundancy. It would be correct if the stem described prolapse.

options.text: Right ventricular dilation from pulmonary embolism
options.rationale: Right ventricular dilation from pulmonary embolism is unrelated to chronic mitral regurgitation; it would be correct if there were acute pulmonary embolic events causing RV strain.

options.text: Annular calcification producing fixed stenotic orifice
options.rationale: Annular calcification can cause valvular dysfunction but is not the typical remodeling pattern of LV volume overload; it would be correct if the primary pathology were mitral annular calcification causing stenosis.

question: Which valvular lesion most commonly predisposes to right-sided infective endocarditis in intravenous drug users?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the pathogenesis, etiologies, predisposing factors, diagnostic criteria and gross/histologic findings of infective endocarditis

options.text: Tricuspid valve infective endocarditis from IV drug use
options.rationale: Intravenous drug use commonly seeds the tricuspid valve leading to right-sided infective endocarditis, as noted in the lecture's predisposing factors.

options.text: Mitral valve prolapse causing left-sided endocarditis
options.rationale: Mitral valve prolapse predisposes to left-sided endocarditis but is not the classic lesion in IV drug users who more often develop tricuspid involvement; it would be correct if the patient had left-sided symptoms and risk factors.

options.text: Aortic stenosis with calcific nodules causing infection
options.rationale: Aortic stenosis can predispose to infective endocarditis but is less associated with IV drug use and right-sided infection; it would be correct if the patient had aortic valve disease and bacteremia.

options.text: Libman-Sacks sterile vegetations in systemic lupus
options.rationale: Libman-Sacks vegetations are sterile and associated with SLE, not IV drug use; they would be correct if the patient had SLE with sterile valvular lesions.

options.text: Nonbacterial thrombotic vegetations from adenocarcinoma
options.rationale: NBTE occurs in hypercoagulable states like mucinous adenocarcinoma and produces sterile vegetations, not the infectious lesions typical in IV drug users; it would be correct if malignancy and embolic phenomena were present.

question: Which echocardiographic finding fulfills a major Duke criterion for infective endocarditis?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the pathogenesis, etiologies, predisposing factors, diagnostic criteria and gross/histologic findings of infective endocarditis

options.text: Oscillating intracardiac mass on valve consistent vegetation
options.rationale: An abnormal echocardiogram showing an oscillating intracardiac mass on a valve consistent with vegetation is a major Duke criterion for infective endocarditis, per the lecture.

options.text: Mild valvular thickening without mobile mass
options.rationale: Mild valvular thickening without a mobile mass is nonspecific and does not meet the major echocardiographic criterion; it would be correct only if a vegetation or abscess were visualized.

options.text: Left ventricular hypertrophy without valvular lesion
options.rationale: Left ventricular hypertrophy is not an echocardiographic sign of endocarditis; it would be correct if the question asked about pressure overload consequences rather than infection.

options.text: Pericardial effusion with fibrinous strands only
options.rationale: Pericardial effusion is not a Duke major criterion for endocarditis; it would be correct if the infection extended to cause pericarditis with echocardiographic evidence of abscess.

options.text: Calcific nodules at leaflet bases without motion
options.rationale: Calcific nodules without motion suggest degenerative valvular disease rather than active infective vegetations; it would be correct if the clinical context favored degenerative stenosis rather than infection.

question: Which lesion is most likely to produce a holosystolic blowing murmur heard best at the apex?
cited_learning_objective: Outline the pathogenesis, etiologies, and clinical and morphologic findings of aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation, mitral valve prolapse, mitral regurgitation, and mitral stenosis

options.text: Mitral regurgitation from leaflet or chordal dysfunction
options.rationale: Mitral regurgitation produces a holosystolic blowing murmur best heard at the apex and radiating to the axilla, often due to leaflet disease or chordal rupture, as described in the lecture.

options.text: Aortic regurgitation producing early diastolic decrescendo murmur
options.rationale: Aortic regurgitation causes an early diastolic decrescendo murmur, not a holosystolic apical blowing murmur; it would be correct if diastolic findings and wide pulse pressure were present.

options.text: Mitral stenosis causing diastolic rumble with opening snap
options.rationale: Mitral stenosis causes a diastolic rumble with an opening snap after S2, not a holosystolic murmur; it would be correct if the stem described diastolic rather than systolic findings.

options.text: Tricuspid stenosis producing systolic ejection murmur
options.rationale: Tricuspid stenosis produces diastolic murmurs and right-sided findings, not a holosystolic apical blowing murmur; it would be correct if right-sided diastolic features were present.

options.text: Aortic stenosis with crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur
options.rationale: Aortic stenosis causes a systolic ejection crescendo-decrescendo murmur radiating to the carotids, not a holosystolic apical blowing murmur; it would be correct if carotid radiation and systolic ejection click were noted.

question: Which mechanism best explains functional mitral regurgitation in dilated cardiomyopathy?
cited_learning_objective: Understand the basic principles of stenotic and regurgitant valvular lesions

options.text: Papillary muscle displacement causing incomplete leaflet coaptation
options.rationale: Ventricular dilation displaces papillary muscles outward and downward, preventing leaflet coaptation and causing functional mitral regurgitation, as explained in the lecture under functional regurgitation.

options.text: Primary leaflet myxomatous degeneration causing prolapse
options.rationale: Primary myxomatous degeneration causes structural leaflet prolapse, not functional regurgitation from ventricular dilation; it would be correct if leaflet histology showed proteoglycan accumulation and redundancy.

options.text: Commissural fusion producing fixed stenotic orifice
options.rationale: Commissural fusion causes mitral stenosis rather than functional regurgitation; it would be correct if the valve leaflets were fibrosed and fused from rheumatic disease.

options.text: Aortic root dilation leading to annular separation
options.rationale: Aortic root dilation affects aortic valve competence and can cause aortic regurgitation, not mitral regurgitation; it would be correct if the mitral annulus were secondarily affected by annular dilation.

options.text: Nonbacterial thrombotic vegetations preventing leaflet motion
options.rationale: NBTE produces small sterile vegetations but typically does not cause the annular dilation and papillary displacement seen in functional regurgitation; it would be correct if large sterile thrombi mechanically impeded leaflet motion.

question: Which clinical sign is most suggestive of acute severe aortic regurgitation rather than chronic regurgitation?
cited_learning_objective: Outline the pathogenesis, etiologies, and clinical and morphologic findings of aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation, mitral valve prolapse, mitral regurgitation, and mitral stenosis

options.text: Sudden pulmonary edema with hypotension and shock
options.rationale: Acute severe aortic regurgitation leads to abrupt volume overload without compensatory LV dilation, causing pulmonary edema, hypotension, and cardiogenic shock, distinguishing it from chronic compensated regurgitation as taught in the lecture.

options.text: Gradual exertional dyspnea with wide pulse pressure
options.rationale: Gradual exertional dyspnea with wide pulse pressure is typical of chronic aortic regurgitation after compensatory LV dilation, not the acute presentation; it would be correct if the history were chronic rather than sudden.

options.text: Mid-systolic click followed by late systolic murmur
options.rationale: A mid-systolic click with late systolic murmur indicates mitral valve prolapse, not acute aortic regurgitation; it would be correct if auscultation revealed a click and late murmur.

options.text: Fever with large friable vegetations on valve
options.rationale: Fever with large friable vegetations suggests infective endocarditis which can cause acute regurgitation but the key distinguishing acute AR sign is hemodynamic collapse; it would be correct if infection were documented as the cause.

options.text: Diastolic rumble with opening snap after S2
options.rationale: A diastolic rumble with opening snap is characteristic of mitral stenosis, not acute aortic regurgitation; it would be correct if mitral valve pathology were present.

question: Which statement best differentiates NBTE from infective endocarditis on valve histology?
cited_learning_objective: Briefly review nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis (NBTE) and Libman-Sacks endocarditis and their associations

options.text: NBTE shows bland thrombus with minimal inflammation
options.rationale: NBTE is characterized by sterile, loosely attached thrombi with little inflammation, distinguishing it from infective endocarditis which shows organisms and neutrophilic inflammation, as the lecture notes.

options.text: Infective endocarditis shows sterile vegetations without organisms
options.rationale: Infective endocarditis typically shows organisms within vegetations and abundant inflammation; sterile vegetations without organisms describe NBTE or Libman-Sacks, not infective endocarditis.

options.text: NBTE always causes valve leaflet destruction and abscess
options.rationale: NBTE usually does not cause destructive changes or abscess formation; such destructive lesions are characteristic of acute infective endocarditis and would make this option correct only in that different context.

options.text: Libman-Sacks vegetations are large friable infected masses
options.rationale: Libman-Sacks vegetations are small sterile vegetations associated with SLE, not large friable infected masses; this option would be correct only if the vegetations were infected, which contradicts Libman-Sacks pathology.

options.text: NBTE is associated with high fever and leukocytosis
options.rationale: NBTE is typically sterile and associated with hypercoagulable states rather than systemic infection signs like fever and leukocytosis; it would be correct if a superimposed infection were present.

question: Which valve abnormality is most commonly affected in chronic rheumatic heart disease?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the pathogenesis, etiologies, predisposing factors, diagnostic criteria and gross/histologic findings of infective endocarditis

options.text: Mitral valve involvement alone is most common
options.rationale: Chronic rheumatic heart disease most commonly affects the mitral valve alone (about 50% of cases), producing leaflet thickening and commissural fusion, as stated in the lecture.

options.text: Aortic valve involvement alone is most common
options.rationale: Aortic valve alone is less commonly the sole valve involved; combined mitral and aortic involvement is common. This option would be correct only if epidemiology favored isolated aortic disease.

options.text: Tricuspid valve involvement predominates in adults
options.rationale: Tricuspid valve involvement is uncommon (about 5%) in rheumatic disease; it would be correct only if the patient had right-sided rheumatic manifestations, which are rare.

options.text: Pulmonic valve involvement is the usual presentation
options.rationale: Pulmonic valve involvement is rare in rheumatic heart disease; this would be correct only in exceptional cases with isolated pulmonic pathology.

options.text: All four valves are equally affected in most cases
options.rationale: Rheumatic disease does not equally affect all valves; mitral involvement is most common. This option would be correct only if data showed equal distribution, which the lecture does not support.

question: Which clinical feature is part of the Jones major criteria for acute rheumatic fever?
cited_learning_objective: List the diagnostic criteria of acute rheumatic fever; describe the pathogenesis and gross/histologic findings of acute and chronic rheumatic heart disease

options.text: Migratory polyarthritis of large joints is a major criterion
options.rationale: Migratory polyarthritis affecting large joints is one of the major Jones criteria for acute rheumatic fever, as listed in the lecture.

options.text: Low grade fever is a major Jones criterion
options.rationale: Fever is a minor criterion in the Jones schema, not a major one; it would be correct only if reclassified as major, which contradicts the established criteria.

options.text: Osler nodes are a major Jones criterion
options.rationale: Osler nodes are associated with infective endocarditis and are not part of the Jones criteria for rheumatic fever; this would be correct only in the context of bacterial endocarditis.

options.text: Prolonged QT interval is a major Jones criterion
options.rationale: A prolonged PR interval (not QT) is a minor criterion in rheumatic fever; this option is incorrect and would be correct only if the ECG finding were a prolonged PR interval and classified differently.

options.text: Subcutaneous nodules are a minor Jones criterion
options.rationale: Subcutaneous nodules are actually a major Jones criterion; this option would be correct only if nodules were misclassified as minor, which is inconsistent with the criteria.

question: Which valvular lesion is most likely to produce microangiopathic hemolytic anemia with schistocytes?
cited_learning_objective: Outline the pathogenesis, etiologies, and clinical and morphologic findings of aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation, mitral valve prolapse, mitral regurgitation, and mitral stenosis

options.text: Severe aortic stenosis causing high shear stress hemolysis
options.rationale: Severe aortic stenosis produces high shear forces across a narrowed orifice leading to red cell fragmentation and schistocytes, as noted in the lecture's complications.

options.text: Chronic mitral regurgitation causing low shear hemolysis
options.rationale: Chronic mitral regurgitation causes volume overload but not the high shear stress that fragments erythrocytes; it would be correct only if there were prosthetic valve or high-velocity jets causing shear.

options.text: Libman-Sacks vegetations causing immune hemolysis
options.rationale: Libman-Sacks vegetations are sterile and associated with SLE; they do not typically cause microangiopathic hemolysis. It would be correct if immune-mediated hemolysis were documented.

options.text: Nonbacterial thrombotic vegetations causing hemolysis
options.rationale: NBTE produces bland thrombi and embolic risk but not classic microangiopathic hemolysis; it would be correct if large valvular thrombi created high shear forces similar to prosthetic valves.

options.text: Aortic regurgitation producing diastolic shear fragmentation
options.rationale: Aortic regurgitation is a diastolic lesion causing volume overload rather than high shear fragmentation; it would be correct only if regurgitant jets produced focal high-velocity shear comparable to stenosis.

question: Which association is classically linked to Streptococcus bovis bacteremia in endocarditis patients?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the pathogenesis, etiologies, predisposing factors, diagnostic criteria and gross/histologic findings of infective endocarditis

options.text: Underlying colorectal carcinoma association with S bovis
options.rationale: Streptococcus bovis bacteremia and endocarditis are classically associated with underlying colorectal carcinoma, a point highlighted in the lecture's etiology slide.

options.text: Prosthetic valve infection from Staphylococcus epidermidis
options.rationale: Staphylococcus epidermidis is associated with prosthetic valve endocarditis, not S. bovis; this option would be correct if the organism identified were S. epidermidis and a prosthetic valve present.

options.text: HACEK organisms causing culture positive endocarditis
options.rationale: HACEK organisms are fastidious and associated with endocarditis but are distinct from S. bovis and not specifically linked to colorectal carcinoma; it would be correct if HACEK organisms were isolated.

options.text: IV drug use causing tricuspid S bovis infection
options.rationale: IV drug use commonly causes Staphylococcus aureus tricuspid endocarditis, not S. bovis; it would be correct if the organism were S. aureus and right-sided involvement present.

options.text: Mucormycosis in immunocompromised hosts causing endocarditis
options.rationale: Mucormycosis is a fungal infection in immunocompromised patients and is not the classic association with S. bovis bacteremia; it would be correct if fungal elements were identified on culture or histology.

question: Which gross description best matches infective endocarditis vegetations?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the pathogenesis, etiologies, predisposing factors, diagnostic criteria and gross/histologic findings of infective endocarditis

options.text: Large friable irregular masses often causing destruction
options.rationale: Infective endocarditis typically produces large, friable, irregular vegetations that can destroy valve tissue and embolize, as shown in the lecture's gross pathology images.

options.text: Small bland thrombi loosely attached without inflammation
options.rationale: Small bland thrombi describe NBTE which lacks inflammation and is sterile, not infective endocarditis; it would be correct if the context were hypercoagulable states rather than infection.

options.text: Small sterile verrucous vegetations along closure line
options.rationale: Small sterile verrucae are characteristic of acute rheumatic fever or Libman-Sacks endocarditis, not infective endocarditis; it would be correct if the patient had ARF or SLE.

options.text: Interchordal ballooning of leaflet tissue resembling parachute
options.rationale: Interchordal ballooning describes mitral valve prolapse grossly, not infective vegetations; it would be correct if the stem described prolapse with hooding leaflets.

options.text: Commissural fusion producing buttonhole stenotic orifice
options.rationale: Commissural fusion and 'buttonhole' stenosis are features of chronic rheumatic mitral stenosis, not infective endocarditis; it would be correct if chronic rheumatic changes were the focus.

question: Which clinical scenario most strongly suggests Libman-Sacks endocarditis rather than infective endocarditis?
cited_learning_objective: Briefly review nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis (NBTE) and Libman-Sacks endocarditis and their associations

options.text: Young patient with systemic lupus and sterile vegetations
options.rationale: Libman-Sacks endocarditis occurs in SLE and produces small sterile vegetations on either surface of the mitral valve; sterile vegetations in an SLE patient point to Libman-Sacks rather than infective endocarditis, per the lecture.

options.text: Fever, positive blood cultures, and large friable vegetations
options.rationale: Fever with positive blood cultures and large friable vegetations indicates infective endocarditis, not Libman-Sacks; it would be correct if organisms were isolated and systemic infection signs present.

options.text: Debilitated cancer patient with bland thrombotic vegetations
options.rationale: A debilitated cancer patient with bland thrombi suggests NBTE associated with mucinous adenocarcinoma, not Libman-Sacks; it would be correct if the patient had malignancy and hypercoagulability.

options.text: Prosthetic valve with Staphylococcus epidermidis infection
options.rationale: Prosthetic valve infection by S. epidermidis is classic for prosthetic infective endocarditis, not Libman-Sacks; it would be correct if a prosthetic valve and positive cultures were present.

options.text: Acute rheumatic fever with verrucous vegetations and fever
options.rationale: Acute rheumatic fever produces small verrucous vegetations and systemic signs but is immunologically mediated post-streptococcal disease, not Libman-Sacks; it would be correct if there were recent streptococcal pharyngitis and Jones criteria met.

question: Which anatomic congenital valve abnormality predisposes to earlier calcific aortic stenosis?
cited_learning_objective: Outline the pathogenesis, etiologies, and clinical and morphologic findings of aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation, mitral valve prolapse, mitral regurgitation, and mitral stenosis

options.text: Congenital bicuspid aortic valve with raphe and unequal cusps
options.rationale: A congenital bicuspid aortic valve with unequal cusps and a raphe predisposes to early calcification and stenosis, as described in the lecture's section on bicuspid valves.

options.text: Tricuspid aortic valve with normal cusp separation
options.rationale: A normal tricuspid aortic valve is less likely to calcify early; it would be correct only if age-related degenerative changes occurred later in life.

options.text: Mitral valve cleft causing regurgitation and prolapse
options.rationale: A mitral valve cleft affects the mitral valve leading to regurgitation or prolapse, not early aortic stenosis; it would be correct if the question targeted mitral pathology.

options.text: Quadricuspid aortic valve causing immediate stenosis at birth
options.rationale: Quadricuspid aortic valves are rare and do not typically cause immediate stenosis at birth; it would be correct only if congenital obstruction were documented neonatally.

options.text: Prosthetic valve degeneration causing early stenosis
options.rationale: Prosthetic valve degeneration can cause stenosis but is an acquired, not congenital, predisposition; it would be correct if the patient had a prosthetic valve history.

question: Which management step is most appropriate for a patient with suspected infective endocarditis and persistent bacteremia?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the pathogenesis, etiologies, predisposing factors, diagnostic criteria and gross/histologic findings of infective endocarditis

options.text: Obtain transesophageal echocardiography to evaluate vegetations
options.rationale: In suspected infective endocarditis with persistent bacteremia, transesophageal echocardiography is the preferred imaging to detect vegetations or abscesses and fulfills a major diagnostic criterion, as emphasized in the lecture.

options.text: Start anticoagulation immediately to prevent embolic events
options.rationale: Immediate anticoagulation is not routinely indicated and may increase bleeding risk with infected vegetations; it would be correct only in specific thromboembolic contexts after multidisciplinary evaluation.

options.text: Perform colonoscopy to search for colorectal carcinoma
options.rationale: Colonoscopy is indicated when Streptococcus bovis is isolated, but it is not the immediate next step for persistent bacteremia; it would be correct if blood cultures specifically grew S. bovis.

options.text: Schedule urgent valve replacement without imaging confirmation
options.rationale: Urgent surgery may be required for complications but imaging confirmation and multidisciplinary assessment are needed before valve replacement; it would be correct if there were heart failure, uncontrolled infection, or large mobile vegetations with embolic events.

options.text: Discharge home with oral antibiotics and outpatient follow up
options.rationale: Discharging with oral antibiotics is inappropriate for persistent bacteremia and suspected endocarditis; it would be correct only if cultures were negative and clinical suspicion was low.

question: Which morphologic change is characteristic of myxomatous mitral valve disease on histology?
cited_learning_objective: Outline the pathogenesis, etiologies, and clinical and morphologic findings of aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation, mitral valve prolapse, mitral regurgitation, and mitral stenosis

options.text: Proteoglycan accumulation with myxoid extracellular matrix
options.rationale: Myxomatous degeneration shows proteoglycan accumulation and mucoid change in the valve leaflet extracellular matrix, producing thickened, redundant leaflets as described in the lecture histology slide.

options.text: Dense calcific nodules at leaflet attachment margins
options.rationale: Dense calcific nodules at attachment margins describe mitral annular calcification or degenerative aortic disease, not myxomatous change; it would be correct if calcification rather than proteoglycan deposition were present.

options.text: Fibrinoid necrosis with Aschoff body formation
options.rationale: Fibrinoid necrosis and Aschoff bodies are features of rheumatic myocarditis, not myxomatous mitral valve disease; it would be correct if acute rheumatic fever were the pathology.

options.text: Bacterial colonies embedded in neutrophilic infiltrate
options.rationale: Bacterial colonies with neutrophils indicate infective endocarditis, not myxomatous degeneration; it would be correct if cultures and histology showed organisms.

options.text: Organized bland thrombus without inflammatory cells
options.rationale: An organized bland thrombus describes NBTE, not myxomatous valve histology; it would be correct if sterile thrombi were found on valve surfaces in a hypercoagulable patient.

question: Which clinical history most strongly suggests chronic rheumatic mitral stenosis rather than acute rheumatic fever?
cited_learning_objective: List the diagnostic criteria of acute rheumatic fever; describe the pathogenesis and gross/histologic findings of acute and chronic rheumatic heart disease

options.text: Decades of progressive exertional dyspnea and hemoptysis
options.rationale: Chronic rheumatic mitral stenosis develops years to decades after acute rheumatic fever and presents with progressive exertional dyspnea, pulmonary congestion, and sometimes hemoptysis due to pulmonary hypertension, matching the lecture description.

options.text: Two weeks of fever and migratory polyarthritis after pharyngitis
options.rationale: Fever and migratory polyarthritis occurring weeks after streptococcal pharyngitis suggest acute rheumatic fever, not chronic rheumatic stenosis; it would be correct if the question asked about the acute phase.

options.text: Sudden onset chest pain with ST elevation on ECG
options.rationale: Sudden chest pain with ST elevation indicates acute myocardial infarction, not chronic rheumatic mitral stenosis; it would be correct if coronary ischemia were the clinical issue.

options.text: Young patient with SLE and sterile mitral vegetations
options.rationale: SLE with sterile vegetations suggests Libman-Sacks endocarditis, not chronic rheumatic mitral stenosis; it would be correct if autoimmune disease and sterile vegetations were documented.

options.text: Acute severe regurgitation with pulmonary edema and hypotension
options.rationale: Acute severe regurgitation presents with sudden pulmonary edema and hypotension, characteristic of acute valvular failure rather than chronic rheumatic stenosis; it would be correct if acute valvular incompetence were present.

question: Which valve lesion is most likely to produce an opening snap on auscultation?
cited_learning_objective: Outline the pathogenesis, etiologies, and clinical and morphologic findings of aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation, mitral valve prolapse, mitral regurgitation, and mitral stenosis

options.text: Mitral stenosis with stiff fused valve leaflets
options.rationale: An opening snap after S2 is characteristic of mitral stenosis due to stiff, fused leaflets from chronic rheumatic disease, as noted in the lecture.

options.text: Aortic regurgitation producing early diastolic decrescendo murmur
options.rationale: Aortic regurgitation causes an early diastolic decrescendo murmur and wide pulse pressure, not an opening snap; it would be correct if diastolic findings were the focus.

options.text: Mitral valve prolapse causing mid-systolic click
options.rationale: Mitral valve prolapse causes a mid-systolic click, not an opening snap; it would be correct if the stem described a click and late systolic murmur.

options.text: Tricuspid regurgitation producing holosystolic murmur
options.rationale: Tricuspid regurgitation produces a holosystolic murmur, not an opening snap; it would be correct if right-sided holosystolic findings were present.

options.text: Nonbacterial thrombotic vegetations causing diastolic click
options.rationale: NBTE does not typically cause an opening snap or diastolic click; it would be correct only if large sterile vegetations mechanically produced an abnormal sound, which is uncommon.

question: Which etiologic factor is listed as a cause of aortic regurgitation in the lecture slides?
cited_learning_objective: Outline the pathogenesis, etiologies, and clinical and morphologic findings of aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation, mitral valve prolapse, mitral regurgitation, and mitral stenosis

options.text: Aortic dissection causing leaflet separation and regurgitation
options.rationale: Aortic dissection can disrupt the aortic root and valve leaflet coaptation causing acute aortic regurgitation, and it is listed among causes in the lecture.

options.text: Mitral annular calcification causing isolated aortic stenosis
options.rationale: Mitral annular calcification affects the mitral valve and may cause mitral dysfunction, not isolated aortic regurgitation; it would be correct only if the aortic valve or root were involved.

options.text: Myxomatous degeneration causing aortic leaflet ballooning
options.rationale: Myxomatous degeneration primarily affects the mitral valve causing prolapse, not aortic leaflet ballooning; it would be correct if histology showed proteoglycan accumulation in aortic leaflets, which is atypical.

options.text: Rheumatic commissural fusion producing aortic stenosis
options.rationale: Rheumatic commissural fusion typically causes mitral stenosis and can affect the aortic valve causing stenosis, not regurgitation; it would be correct if the question targeted aortic stenosis from rheumatic disease.

options.text: Libman-Sacks sterile vegetations causing acute regurgitation
options.rationale: Libman-Sacks vegetations are sterile and usually small; they can cause regurgitation but are not a primary listed cause of aortic regurgitation in the lecture. It would be correct if SLE-related valvulopathy produced significant regurgitation.

question: Which complication is most likely when large friable vegetations embolize from left-sided infective endocarditis?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the pathogenesis, etiologies, predisposing factors, diagnostic criteria and gross/histologic findings of infective endocarditis

options.text: Systemic arterial emboli causing infarction in organs
options.rationale: Left-sided infective endocarditis vegetations can embolize to systemic arteries causing infarction in brain, spleen, kidney, or other organs, as discussed in the lecture's complications.

options.text: Pulmonary embolism from right-sided valvular vegetations
options.rationale: Pulmonary embolism results from right-sided vegetations embolizing to the lungs, not left-sided lesions; it would be correct if the infection involved the tricuspid valve.

options.text: Coronary artery thrombosis causing myocardial infarction
options.rationale: Embolization to coronary arteries is possible but less common; systemic emboli more typically affect brain and spleen. This option would be correct if there were clinical evidence of coronary embolus.

options.text: Deep venous thrombosis from sterile valvular thrombi
options.rationale: Deep venous thrombosis arises from venous thrombi, not embolization of left-sided valvular vegetations; it would be correct if venous thrombi were documented.

options.text: Right heart failure from left atrial thrombus burden
options.rationale: Right heart failure from left atrial thrombus is not a direct consequence of left-sided vegetations; it would be correct only if secondary pulmonary hypertension developed over time causing right heart strain.

question: Which feature distinguishes acute from subacute infective endocarditis clinically?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the pathogenesis, etiologies, predisposing factors, diagnostic criteria and gross/histologic findings of infective endocarditis

options.text: Rapid progression with highly virulent organisms in acute disease
options.rationale: Acute infective endocarditis is rapidly progressive due to highly virulent organisms often on previously normal valves, whereas subacute is indolent with less virulent organisms on damaged valves, as the lecture explains.

options.text: Indolent course with normal valves in subacute disease
options.rationale: Subacute endocarditis typically occurs on previously damaged valves and has an indolent course; this option is incorrect about valve status and would be correct only if valve condition were normal.

options.text: Fever absent in acute disease but present in subacute
options.rationale: Fever is common in both acute and subacute endocarditis; absence of fever in acute disease is not a distinguishing feature. It would be correct only in atypical presentations.

options.text: Culture negativity defines acute infective endocarditis
options.rationale: Culture negativity is not a defining feature of acute disease; culture-negative endocarditis may occur with fastidious organisms in subacute cases. This option would be correct only if cultures failed to grow organisms.

options.text: Presence of Osler nodes only in subacute presentations
options.rationale: Osler nodes can occur in both forms and are not exclusive to subacute disease; this would be correct only if Osler nodes were proven to be absent in acute cases, which is not the case.

question: Which valve pathology is most likely to cause pulmonary hypertension and right-sided heart failure over time?
cited_learning_objective: Outline the pathogenesis, etiologies, and clinical and morphologic findings of aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation, mitral valve prolapse, mitral regurgitation, and mitral stenosis

options.text: Mitral stenosis causing left atrial hypertension and pulmonary congestion
options.rationale: Mitral stenosis leads to left atrial dilation and elevated pulmonary venous pressures, causing pulmonary hypertension and eventual right-sided heart failure, as described in the lecture.

options.text: Aortic stenosis causing isolated right ventricular pressure overload
options.rationale: Aortic stenosis primarily causes left ventricular pressure overload and does not directly cause pulmonary hypertension; it would be correct only if secondary left heart failure led to pulmonary hypertension.

options.text: Tricuspid regurgitation causing left atrial enlargement
options.rationale: Tricuspid regurgitation affects right-sided chambers and does not cause left atrial enlargement; it would be correct if right-sided volume overload affected left heart indirectly, which is uncommon.

options.text: Aortic regurgitation producing pulmonary venous hypertension
options.rationale: Aortic regurgitation causes LV volume overload and may lead to heart failure but is less directly associated with pulmonary hypertension than mitral stenosis; it would be correct if severe LV failure caused secondary pulmonary hypertension.

options.text: Nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis causing pulmonary emboli
options.rationale: NBTE can embolize but systemic emboli are more typical; pulmonary emboli would result from right-sided lesions and venous thrombi, not NBTE on left-sided valves. It would be correct if right-sided NBTE were present.

question: Which diagnostic test is most sensitive for detecting small vegetations on prosthetic valves?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the pathogenesis, etiologies, predisposing factors, diagnostic criteria and gross/histologic findings of infective endocarditis

options.text: Transesophageal echocardiography provides superior sensitivity
options.rationale: Transesophageal echocardiography offers higher resolution and sensitivity for detecting vegetations and perivalvular abscesses, especially on prosthetic valves, and is recommended in suspected endocarditis per the lecture's diagnostic emphasis.

options.text: Transthoracic echocardiography is most sensitive for prosthetics
options.rationale: Transthoracic echocardiography has lower sensitivity for prosthetic valve vegetations due to acoustic shadowing; it would be correct only for large vegetations in favorable windows.

options.text: Blood culture negativity rules out prosthetic valve infection
options.rationale: Negative blood cultures do not exclude prosthetic valve infection, especially with prior antibiotics or fastidious organisms; it would be correct only if cultures were repeatedly and appropriately negative and imaging also normal.

options.text: Chest radiograph reliably visualizes valvular vegetations
options.rationale: Chest radiograph cannot visualize valvular vegetations; it would be correct only if there were large calcifications or prosthetic hardware visible, not vegetations.

options.text: Electrocardiogram demonstrates vegetations as electrical changes
options.rationale: ECG does not detect vegetations; it may show conduction abnormalities if infection extends to conduction tissue. It would be correct only if perivalvular abscess caused new conduction defects.

question: Which therapeutic consideration is most important when managing a patient with severe symptomatic aortic stenosis?
cited_learning_objective: Outline the pathogenesis, etiologies, and clinical and morphologic findings of aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation, mitral valve prolapse, mitral regurgitation, and mitral stenosis

options.text: Evaluate for valve replacement due to symptomatic severe obstruction
options.rationale: Symptomatic severe aortic stenosis often requires valve replacement because medical therapy does not relieve the fixed obstruction; the lecture emphasizes the progressive nature and poor prognosis without intervention.

options.text: Begin high dose diuretics as definitive long term therapy
options.rationale: Diuretics may relieve congestion but do not correct the fixed valvular obstruction and are not definitive long-term therapy; it would be correct only as temporary symptomatic management before definitive intervention.

options.text: Immediate anticoagulation to prevent valve calcification progression
options.rationale: Anticoagulation does not prevent calcific degeneration of aortic valves and is not indicated for that purpose; it would be correct only if there were another indication such as atrial fibrillation.

options.text: Administer broad spectrum antifungals empirically
options.rationale: Empiric antifungals are not indicated for degenerative aortic stenosis; they would be correct only if fungal endocarditis were suspected with supporting evidence.

options.text: Refer for percutaneous mitral balloon commissurotomy
options.rationale: Percutaneous balloon commissurotomy treats mitral stenosis, not aortic stenosis; it would be correct if the patient had rheumatic mitral stenosis with suitable valve morphology.

question: Which pathologic process underlies the formation of verrucae on valve leaflets in acute rheumatic fever?
cited_learning_objective: List the diagnostic criteria of acute rheumatic fever; describe the pathogenesis and gross/histologic findings of acute and chronic rheumatic heart disease

options.text: Fibrinoid necrosis with small inflammatory vegetations along closure
options.rationale: Verrucae in acute rheumatic fever represent small inflammatory vegetations with fibrinoid necrosis along the line of valve closure, as described in the lecture's valve disease slides.

options.text: Proteoglycan accumulation causing myxomatous leaflet ballooning
options.rationale: Proteoglycan accumulation causes myxomatous degeneration and prolapse, not verrucous inflammatory vegetations; it would be correct if the pathology were mitral valve prolapse.

options.text: Bland sterile thrombus formation without inflammation
options.rationale: Bland sterile thrombi characterize NBTE and lack inflammation, unlike the inflammatory verrucae of acute rheumatic fever; it would be correct if the vegetations were sterile and noninflammatory.

options.text: Bacterial colonization with neutrophilic abscess formation
options.rationale: Bacterial colonization with neutrophils indicates infective endocarditis rather than rheumatic verrucae; it would be correct if cultures and histology demonstrated organisms.

options.text: Calcific degeneration producing nodular hard masses
options.rationale: Calcific degeneration produces nodular calcific masses typical of degenerative aortic stenosis, not the small inflammatory verrucae of acute rheumatic fever; it would be correct if calcification were the dominant process.

question: Which clinical feature from the lecture increases suspicion for infective endocarditis in a febrile patient with a new murmur?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the pathogenesis, etiologies, predisposing factors, diagnostic criteria and gross/histologic findings of infective endocarditis

options.text: Fever plus new murmur should prompt evaluation for endocarditis
options.rationale: The lecture explicitly states that fever with a new murmur should be considered infective endocarditis until proven otherwise, making this combination a key clinical trigger for further workup.

options.text: Isolated fatigue without fever rules out infective endocarditis
options.rationale: Isolated fatigue without fever does not rule out endocarditis, especially in subacute or immunocompromised patients; it would be correct only if there were no other supporting signs or risk factors.

options.text: Presence of erythema marginatum indicates bacterial endocarditis
options.rationale: Erythema marginatum is a Jones major criterion for rheumatic fever, not a sign of bacterial endocarditis; it would be correct only in the context of post-streptococcal rheumatic disease.

options.text: New murmur in absence of bacteremia excludes endocarditis
options.rationale: A new murmur without documented bacteremia does not exclude endocarditis; blood cultures may be negative early or with prior antibiotics. It would be correct only if multiple cultures and imaging were negative.

options.text: Janeway lesions are pathognomonic and always present
options.rationale: Janeway lesions are a minor sign and not always present; they support but do not definitively diagnose endocarditis. This option would be correct only if pathognomonic signs were universally present, which they are not.

question: Which valve abnormality is most commonly associated with systemic embolization of sterile thrombi in malignancy?
cited_learning_objective: Briefly review nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis (NBTE) and Libman-Sacks endocarditis and their associations

options.text: Nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis with bland sterile vegetations
options.rationale: NBTE is associated with mucinous adenocarcinomas and hypercoagulable states and produces bland sterile vegetations that can embolize systemically, as described in the lecture.

options.text: Libman-Sacks endocarditis in systemic lupus causing emboli
options.rationale: Libman-Sacks vegetations in SLE are sterile and can embolize but NBTE in malignancy is the classic association for systemic embolization; this option would be correct if the patient had SLE rather than malignancy.

options.text: Infective endocarditis with bacterial vegetations causing emboli
options.rationale: Infective endocarditis causes emboli but the question asks specifically about sterile thrombi in malignancy, which points to NBTE; it would be correct if organisms were identified.

options.text: Rheumatic verrucae producing large embolic fragments
options.rationale: Rheumatic verrucae are small and inflammatory and less likely to cause large sterile emboli typical of NBTE; it would be correct only in rare circumstances with large vegetations.

options.text: Prosthetic valve pannus formation causing embolization
options.rationale: Pannus formation is fibrous tissue growth on prosthetic valves and is not the classic source of sterile emboli in malignancy; it would be correct if prosthetic valve complications produced embolic debris.

question: Which morphologic description corresponds to calcific aortic stenosis in elderly patients?
cited_learning_objective: Outline the pathogenesis, etiologies, and clinical and morphologic findings of aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation, mitral valve prolapse, mitral regurgitation, and mitral stenosis

options.text: Nodular masses of calcium on valve leaflets sparing edges
options.rationale: Degenerative calcific aortic stenosis in the elderly shows nodular calcific masses on cusps with free edges often spared, as illustrated in the lecture slides.

options.text: Diffuse commissural fusion producing buttonhole mitral orifice
options.rationale: Diffuse commissural fusion and 'buttonhole' orifice describe chronic rheumatic mitral stenosis, not calcific aortic stenosis; it would be correct if mitral valve pathology were the focus.

options.text: Interchordal ballooning with thrombotic plaques on leaflet
options.rationale: Interchordal ballooning with thrombotic plaques is characteristic of mitral valve prolapse, not calcific aortic stenosis; it would be correct if the stem described prolapse findings.

options.text: Small verrucous vegetations along closure line in ARF
options.rationale: Small verrucous vegetations are seen in acute rheumatic fever and are not the calcific nodules of degenerative aortic stenosis; it would be correct if ARF were the pathology.

options.text: Bland thrombotic vegetations loosely attached to cusp surface
options.rationale: Bland thrombotic vegetations describe NBTE and are not the calcific nodules of degenerative aortic stenosis; it would be correct if the patient had a hypercoagulable state with sterile thrombi.

question: Which clinical history would most strongly suggest a diagnosis of acute rheumatic fever rather than infective endocarditis?
cited_learning_objective: List the diagnostic criteria of acute rheumatic fever; describe the pathogenesis and gross/histologic findings of acute and chronic rheumatic heart disease

options.text: Recent streptococcal pharyngitis followed by migratory arthritis
options.rationale: Acute rheumatic fever typically occurs 2–3 weeks after group A streptococcal pharyngitis and presents with migratory polyarthritis and other Jones criteria, distinguishing it from infective endocarditis which presents with bacteremia and vegetations.

options.text: Fever with positive blood cultures and large vegetations
options.rationale: Fever with positive blood cultures and large vegetations is classic for infective endocarditis, not acute rheumatic fever; it would be correct if bacteremia and echocardiographic vegetations were documented.

options.text: SLE patient with sterile mitral vegetations and antiphospholipid antibodies
options.rationale: SLE with sterile vegetations suggests Libman-Sacks endocarditis, not acute rheumatic fever; it would be correct if autoimmune serologies and SLE features were present.

options.text: IV drug user with tricuspid vegetations and septic pulmonary emboli
options.rationale: IV drug use with tricuspid vegetations and septic pulmonary emboli indicates right-sided infective endocarditis, not acute rheumatic fever; it would be correct if the patient had IV drug use history and pulmonary septic emboli.

options.text: Elderly patient with calcific aortic stenosis and angina
options.rationale: An elderly patient with calcific aortic stenosis presents with angina and syncope due to degenerative disease, not acute rheumatic fever; it would be correct if degenerative valve disease were the focus.
